division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.17(1)  For the purpose of conducting a review under this
Division, a review officer may do all or any of the following:
(a) take evidence either by affidavit or orally under oath, or
both;
(b) direct the production of records;
(c) require notice of the appointment for the review to be
served on persons who may be affected by the review or
who have an interest in the trust, estate, fund or property
from which the lawyer’s charges are or may be paid or
charged;
(d) give directions about how notice of the appointment for
the review is to be served;
(e) allow a party to be represented by a lawyer;
(f) require details of a retainer agreement, or of the services
provided, money collected and expended, disbursements
or other charges claimed or any other matter necessary to
understand the agreement or charges and decide whether
the agreement or charges, or both, are reasonable;
(g) validate service of the notice of the appointment or, if
service is impractical or impossible, dispense with
service;
(h) determine the applicability of a time period specified in
these rules in respect of a review conducted under this
Division and extend or shorten an applicable time period.
(2)  A review officer may not review either a retainer agreement or
a lawyer’s charges that have previously been reviewed by a review
officer unless the Court so orders or the parties agree.

BOOK_A.title: Review Ofﬁcer’s Authority
BOOK_A.operative_text_raw:
10.17(1) For the purpose of conducting a review under this Division, a review
ofﬁcer may do all or any of the following:
(a) take evidence either by afﬁdavit or orally under oath, or both;
(b) direct the production of records;
(c) require notice of the appointment for the review to be served on
persons who may be affected by the review or who have an interest
in the trust, estate, fund or property from which the lawyer’s charges
are or may be paid or charged;
(d) give directions about how notice of the appointment for the review is
to be served;
(e) allow a party to be represented by a lawyer;
(f) require details of a retainer agreement, or of the services provided,
money collected and expended, disbursements or other charges
claimed or any other matter necessary to understand the agreement
or charges and decide whether the agreement or charges, or both,
are reasonable;
(g) validate service of the notice of the appointment or, if service is
impractical or impossible, dispense with service.²
(h) determine the applicability of a time period specified in these rules
in respect of a review conducted under this Division and extend or
shorten an applicable time period.
(2) A review ofﬁcer may not review either a retainer agreement or a lawyer’s
charges that have previously been reviewed by a review ofﬁcer unless the Court
so orders or the parties agree.¹
[Alta. Reg.124/10;36/20]
BOOK_A.commentary:
Paragraph 1(h) was added in 2020.
The review is based in part on the ofﬁcer’s expertise.²
On criteria to review a retainer agreement, see R.10.7 nn. E, G, and R.10.9 n.
A review ofﬁcer cannot hear any question about who is liable to pay fees, but he or she can ﬁx
the amount despite such a dispute.³
A review ofﬁcer should hear and decide an application over the propriety and fairness and
amount of a lawyer’s bill, and not adjourn the matter until a negligence suit is decided. The review
ofﬁcer has expertise over fairness and reasonableness of fees, but not over negligence. Here
there was a contingency fee agreement which contract was not disputed, and was clear, and the
law ﬁrm simply sought the percentages in the contract.⁴
Many aspects of the client’s aims, instructions, behavior, communications, and cooperation
with his or her lawyer, are relevant when assessing the proper size of the lawyer’s bill.⁵
An Applications Judge cannot assess the reasonableness of fees or the work done to earn
them, even on a foreclosure suit.⁶
Especially if there is a contract to pay the plaintiff’s legal bills.
The correct procedure is for the review ofﬁcer to review the fees.⁷
Evidence heard by the review ofﬁcer need not be sworn.⁸
The lawyer can give evidence of his
or her own experience, and need not call an independent expert witness.⁹
The review ofﬁcer should not make assumptions about a law ﬁrm’s ability or experience.¹⁰
Nor
about the client’s ﬁnancial situation.¹¹
Where there were relevant disputed fact questions before a review ofﬁcer, he was right to
decline jurisdiction and not review the account, and a chambers judge on appeal was right to

afﬁrm that.¹
But the judge should have provided for a means to decide the fact questions, and so
the Court of Appeal directed trial of an issue as to the terms of the retainer agreement.²
Afﬁdavits on irrelevant topics (such as insurance and ﬁnancial strength) were struck out.³
Apparently all reviews or assessments are digitally sound-recorded on the courts’ “FTR”
system.
Directives of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy are not law, and merely his or her interpretation
of the law.⁴

BOOK_B.title: Review officer's authority

commentary.text: Rule 10.17 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.17. Guidelines for Reviewing Contingency Accounts In Sonnenberg v. Schumacher & Associates, 2005 ABQB 352, 2005 CarswellAlta 840, 52 Alta. L.R. (4th) 151, 16 C.P.C. (6th) 88, Germain J. set out the following guidelines for taxing officers who are called upon to review contingency accounts. At pp. 155–156, his Lordship said: I set out the following guidelines for taxing officers to utilize when reviewing contingency accounts. These guidelines are not exhaustive. First, the taxing officer should attempt in a summary way to come to a final decision on the taxation issue, using the referral power only sparingly, unless the client in fact requests the referral as permitted in Rule 619(2). This is consistent with the summary nature of the proceedings, yet protects the interests of the parties, as the issue may still be reviewed de novo by a judge. Second, the taxing officer should review the contingency agreement against the checklist in Rule 616, inviting the lawyer to point out technical compliance, if required. If the taxing officer is not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that technical compliance has occurred, then the taxing officer should advise the lawyer to justify the account on a quantum meruit basis. That is, the lawyer should have the opportunity to prove that the account is fair even without the benefit of the contingency agreement. On the other hand, if the taxing officer is satisfied that the contingency agreement does comply with the Rules, then the taxing officer should conduct the taxation on the basis that the contingency agreement is highly significant to what the taxing officer should consider. The taxing officer should recognize a fundamental entitlement to legal fees on a contingency, but this should not be the only factor for the taxing officer to consider. Third, when taxing an account to which a valid contingency agreement applies, the taxing officer is free to refer to prior cases of comparable complexity. In relatively routine motor vehicle actions, where liability is not greatly in dispute, a contingency of 25% seems to me to be close to the upper limit, absent unusual circumstances. In more complex litigation, such as medical malpractice, even 50% may pass a taxation. There is an economic reality to legal work, such that the law firm may have a sliding scale, which too may pass taxation. The sliding scale may be based on the number of steps taken, with the largest percentage payable in cases that go to trial and a much lower percentage in cases that settle early in the negotiation stage. In the alternative, the sliding scale may have the percentage higher on the first dollars, but lower as the amount collected increases. The taxing officer may find either approach reasonable. It is clear, however, that the taxing officer must do some analysis of the work effort, the risk, and the result, regardless of any valid contingency agreement. Otherwise, Rule 616(2)(h) would be unnecessary. Fourth, in more complicated taxations, the taxing officer may wish to give reasons, but is free not to do so, in light of the summary nature of taxation. Finally, when the taxing officer uses Rule 619(2) to refer a matter to a judge, the taxing officer and the client can expect the judge to deal with all issues arising in the taxation and not only the narrow issue that motivated the referral, although the judge is free not to conduct such a broad review. This is consistent with the summary and expeditious approach to be taken in the taxation of legal accounts. The alternative, of deciding the narrow issue referred and remitting the matter to the taxing officer, should generally be expected only in complex accounts, where there are numerous mathematical calculations and considerations.
